cues.text: A Governor Turned Bishop by Acclamation
Born around 340 to a distinguished Roman family already marked by Christian martyrdom in earlier generations, Ambrose served as Roman governor of the province centered on Milan.
In 374, the city's Catholic and Arian factions deadlocked over electing a new bishop, threatening violence in the very cathedral.
Ambrose entered the church to calm the crowd with his authority as governor.
In a moment neither he nor anyone present had planned, a child's voice — or, as some accounts have it, the whole assembled crowd — suddenly cried out that Ambrose himself should be their bishop.
Though not yet even baptized and by his own account deeply reluctant, Ambrose was baptized, ordained through each successive clerical rank, and consecrated bishop within the space of about a week.
Learning as He Governed
Thrust so suddenly into an office he had never sought, Ambrose found that his legal, not theological, education had scarcely prepared him for it.
He therefore set himself at once to an intensive study of Scripture and of the Greek Fathers, whose language and works were, fortunately, already familiar to him from his upbringing.
His mastery of Greek theology would give the Latin West, through Ambrose, direct access to a rich tradition it might otherwise have known only secondhand.
Within a remarkably short time, this reluctant, self-taught bishop had become one of the most formidable preachers and pastoral theologians of his age.
His sermons and treatises shaped Latin Christian thought on subjects ranging from the moral duties of the clergy to the meaning of the sacraments.
An Emperor Made to Wait
Ambrose's episcopate is remembered above all for his fearless insistence that even emperors remained subject to the moral authority of the Church.
When the Emperor Theodosius I ordered a brutal massacre of civilians at Thessalonica in 390, Ambrose refused him communion.
The massacre was in retaliation for a riot, and Theodosius, remarkably, submitted to public penance.
He stood among the penitents at the cathedral doors before Ambrose would readmit him to the sacraments.
Earlier still, Ambrose had faced down the Arian empress-regent Justina and the imperial troops sent to seize a Milanese basilica for Arian worship.
He barricaded himself with his congregation inside the church through an entire Holy Week rather than surrender it.

Taken together, these episodes established for the whole of Western Christendom a principle of lasting consequence: that political power, however great, does not extend over the conscience or the sacraments of the Church.
Winning Augustine for Christ
Among the many souls Ambrose's preaching touched, none would prove more consequential for the whole future of Western theology than Augustine .
He was a brilliant, restless young rhetoric teacher from North Africa who came to Milan deeply entangled in Manichaean error and skepticism.
At first, by his own later admission, he attended Ambrose's sermons only to study the bishop's celebrated eloquence rather than to hear his message.

Over many months, almost despite himself, Augustine found Ambrose's preaching slowly dismantling his objections to Christianity, through its careful, allegorical reading of the Old Testament and intellectual seriousness.
This patient process of conversion would culminate in Augustine's baptism by Ambrose's own hand at the Easter Vigil of 387, watched by his mother Monica .
Her own years of prayer had led them both to that same font.
A Hymnwriter and Liturgist
Ambrose left the Western Church another lasting gift beyond his sermons: a body of Latin hymns, sung to melodies of his own devising.
These hymns introduced congregational singing into Milan’s liturgy and helped shape the entire subsequent tradition of Latin Christian hymnody.
The distinct liturgical rite of Milan still bears his name to this day, the Ambrosian Rite, one of the very few Western liturgical traditions never absorbed into the common Roman use.
Legacy
Ambrose died in Milan on 4 April 397, mourned by a city he had governed, in every sense, as both civic leader and shepherd of souls for twenty-three years.
Counted among the four great Doctors of the Latin Church alongside Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory the Great, Ambrose remains the enduring model of the bishop unafraid to speak truth to power.
He proves that a Church which will not bend its moral witness for earthly favor can, in the end, command genuine respect even from emperors it dares to correct.
